Where the idea comes from

Thousands of years of round-boat know-how

The coracle has been used on rivers and coastlines for over 2,000 years: a small, round, light craft that's almost impossible to capsize because it has no corners to catch a wave. Circraft takes that same round, stable hull and adds a pair of skis underneath — so instead of just floating, it lifts and skims across the surface at speed.

The shape that once kept fishermen safe on rough rivers now does something new: it turns choppy water into a fast, fun ride, while keeping the same remarkable stability that made the coracle last for millennia.

For resorts, beach clubs & hire fleets

A safer kind of thrill on the water

No handlebars, no complicated steering wheel — you turn Circraft just by leaning your weight, and it comes round on a sixpence (do those still exist?). That makes it an easy craft to hand to a guest who's never driven anything on water before.

  • ＋Round, enclosed hull is far harder to capsize than a jet ski or SeaDoo — reassuring for resorts managing risk with first-time riders.
  • ＋Body-weight steering means no controls to teach — guests are riding confidently within minutes.
  • ＋Compact footprint next to a full-size jet ski, so more craft fit on the same stretch of beach.
  • ＋Liveries can match resort branding, national flags, or sponsor colours straight out of the mould.
The mechanics

How Circraft works

A round hull for stability, twin skis for speed, and a simple idea borrowed from one of the oldest boats in the world.

From standing start to skimming

Three things make it work

1

The round hull sits stable on the water

Like a coracle, Circraft's disc-shaped hull has no bow or stern to dig in or get swamped side-on. It sits evenly on the water whichever way the waves come from, which is what makes it so hard to capsize or sink.

2

Twin skis lift it onto the surface

As power is applied, a pair of skis underneath the hull generate lift, raising the craft up so it's skimming across the top of the water rather than pushing through it — cutting drag and letting it move fast over chop.

3

The rider stays level and dry

Because the hull rides above the waves instead of through them, the ride stays flatter and drier than a conventional hull — turning rough water into part of the fun instead of a problem to fight.

4

You steer with your body, not a wheel

There's no handlebar or steering wheel to learn. Shift your weight and Circraft comes round on a sixpence — about as simple as controls get, which is exactly why first-timers pick it up in minutes.

The view from behind: twin skis either side of the outboard, doing the lifting.
